record.tranche_reason: The post compares the difference-in-means compliance vector with a separately extracted trust vector, including a trust vector orthogonalized against compliance, and reports that the orthogonalized vector still changes harmful-prompt responses. This refines the account by presenting a distinct route to bypassing safety behavior.
record.gate_note: The post reports outcomes for activation steering with trust and compliance vectors, and for user-description judgments. The manually swept layer/strength choices are setup choices, not outcome rows. Figures 1–10 are referenced but their plotted values are not present in the supplied text; only outcomes described in prose are recorded where possible. The appendix cosine-similarity figures have no stated results.
record.test_reason: The post rebuilds the Arditi difference-in-means vector and steers with it, adding it to cut refusal and subtracting it to induce refusal. It also shows that a trust vector orthogonalized against that vector still bypasses refusal. That bears on V1's addition effects and on whether other directions also govern refusal (V4).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author also reports that trust vectors cut refusal on harmful prompts even more than the compliance vector, and that removing the compliance component does not change their effect. Pivot responses, though counted as compliance, withhold restricted content.
record.recipe_differences: The study computes a harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation compliance vector using the cited method, but uses activation addition at one selected layer rather than ablating the direction across every layer and position. Its trust vectors come from logistic-regression probes on synthetic conversations.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering layer and strength were selected after a manual sweep. Trust and compliance vectors used different layers and strengths across the two models. The text reports that trust-vector effects on benign prompts are especially close to base behavior for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

fits_no_version.finding: Trust-vector steering pushes the model to judge described users trustworthy, even explicitly untrustworthy ones. Negative steering gives evasive open answers or 100% No in Yes/No format; a random vector has no effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A user-trustworthiness direction causally biases a model's explicit judgments of a described user's trustworthiness.

record.problems: Most plotted numerical results are unavailable in the supplied text, and several outcomes are described without exact rates. Experiments use synthetic data; the author notes the trust attribute may instead be a broader contextual shift and that the training scenarios are narrowly scoped. The text gives sample counts for evaluation prompts but reports no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 6–8 compare system prompts and steering conditions, but the supplied text gives captions without outcome descriptions or values, so no outcome rows were extracted. Figures 11–14 report cosine similarities without textual results and are not included.

untested.parts: Directional ablation across all layers and positions; preservation of general capabilities. Steering is single-layer activation addition only.
Affine or cone geometry; whether the orthogonal trust vector still acts through the refusal direction at downstream layers.
Not tested; the author's speculation about benign intent versus harmlessness is not measured.
Not tested; suggested only as future work.

missing.what: Experiment 1 results (compliance, restricted content, style) for Llama-3.1-8B, said to show very similar trends
missing.locator: Experiment 1, link to the companion LessWrong post

missing.what: Effect of HHH and trust system prompts combined with compliance or orthogonal trust steering

record.verdict_notes: The sign convention is ambiguous: the 'compliance vector' is called a difference in means, yet adding it reduces refusal, so it behaves as harmless minus harmful. All results come from figures with no numbers in the text, so states rest on prose descriptions. 'Compliance rate' counts pivot responses, which give no restricted content. No capability checks or uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the difference-in-means direction, test projection at every layer and position, or assess whether general capabilities remain intact. Its compliance-vector steering is at a selected layer.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
No attack that suppresses the direction, or training against its ablation, is tested.

Tests an orthogonalized trust vector as a distinct route and contrasts behavior with compliance steering; it does not test affine or cone geometry, or whether a dominant direction plus other directions is the best description.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or systematic model-variant transfer test.
Does not vary refusal-training method or timing.
No reasoning models are tested; the author suggests this as future work.

relation.reason: It rebuilds the Arditi DiM vector, steers with it in both signs, and reports its own refusal/compliance results. It also tests an orthogonal direction against it.

tranche.reason: The post argues refusal is not a single switch and that there are multiple ways to abliterate. It shows that a trust vector orthogonalized against the rebuilt DiM vector still bypasses refusal, which is a result bearing on whether V1 needs restating.

source_check.notes: The pack gave no [lN] ids, so labels are numbered l1, l2 in pack order. The compliance vector's formula is lost in the text. As used, adding it lowers refusal and adding its negative induces refusal, so it points opposite to Arditi's refusal direction; the recipe's 'harmful-minus-harmless' sign can't be checked. All steering/refusal rates are figure-only; the only numeric table (Table 3) is the trust-perception experiment, not refusal. The authors_conclusion paraphrase is correct.

statements.correction: lw:AExop (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, layer 12, strength 3, 200 HarmBench/JailbreakBench harmful prompts): trust vectors orthogonalized against the compliance vector still give a response on almost every harmful prompt, with more pivot/reframed outputs than the compliance vector; no rates in the text. Steering against the trust vectors on 100 WildJailBreak adversarial benign prompts (3B layer 12; 8B layer 13, refusal-dataset vectors only) leaves refusal very close to base; steering against the compliance vector gives the highest refusal.
statements.problem: The visible parts about this study are right: orthogonality is only at the steering layer, layer and strength came from a manual sweep, it is a LessWrong post with code and controls, it covers two models, there is no capability check, and rates are mostly figure-only. But the 'what' text about this study is cut off at 'Independently fi…', so the finding itself can't be checked. Of the cited rows, only r1 (with r4 as a qualifier) shows a non-DiM direction acting on refusal. r7 and r9 show that steering against the trust vectors leaves benign-prompt refusal near base.

statements.correction: lw:AExop models: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (both under 10B). Adding the negative of the compliance vector clearly leads to excessive refusal on 100 WildJailBreak adversarial benign prompts (highest refusal rate), in both models. Steering against trust vectors stays near base. Single-vector activation addition at one layer only.
statements.problem: Wrong to say lw:AExop r1-r9 all push toward compliance. Per the record's V1 verdict, r6 and r8 subtract the compliance vector and induce refusal on benign prompts. r7 and r9 steer against trust vectors and leave refusal near base. All of these are single-vector steering, not several directions combined, and both models are under 10B. The main point, that nothing tests this above 10B, is not affected by this study.
